fatal_errors: The hypothesis concerns hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10, whereas the target study concerns composition screening and experimental validation in the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system, specifically Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 versus equimolar NbMoTaVW.
It replaces the target's rule-of-mixtures modulus, VEC, and density screening of 38,326 compositions with an unvalidated reduced-order physics-informed active-learning framework.
It proposes tensile and fracture-toughness prediction, while the target's decisive mechanical result was room-temperature quasi-static compression and did not report fracture toughness.
The claimed 15–20% accuracy improvement and greater than 50% computational saving are unsupported by the cited evidence.

The prospective benchmark lacks a specified sample count, processing-variable range, fixed training set, error metric, engineering tolerance, and preregistered baseline, so its falsification rule is not decisive.
explanation: This is not a reconstruction of the target methodology or result. The target used a simple, validated composition-based modulus estimate together with VEC and calculated density to screen Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W compositions, then tested an as-cast selected alloy under compression. Its proposed mechanism was reduced VEC lowering barriers to dislocation motion, producing extensive slip and a fracture strain of 35.7% while retaining high strength. The generated hypothesis instead offers a generic multiscale physics-informed ML concept for a different alloy, microstructure, property set, and test mode. The citations establish only broad facts about computational expense, active learning, descriptor models, and dataset dependence; they do not validate prediction of toughness in HfNbTiVAl10 or the numerical performance claims. The stated applicability limits are reasonable in principle, but the proposed benchmark is too underspecified and circularly tied to unsupported improvement percentages.
